A conical container has a height of $8\,\text{cm},$ and the radius at the bottom of the container is $4\,\text{cm}.$ Batter is being poured into the container. If the level of the batter in the container is increasing at a rate of $\frac{4}{\pi }\,\text{cm/s}$, find the rate at which the volume of the batter is increasing when the radius of the batter surface is $\frac{3}{2}\,\text{cm}.$ Do not round the answer.

The volume of batter is increasing at a rate of
{{field-1}} ${\text{cm}}^{3}/\text{s}.$
question.worked_solution:
First, let's consider the dimensions of the container. Let's call $H=8\,\text{cm}$ the height of the conical container, and $R=4\,\text{cm}$ its radius at the bottom. These quantities are fixed and do not change with time.

Now, let's consider the batter level. We call $h$ the distance from the top of the container to the batter surface, $r$ the radius of the cone at the surface of the batter, and $v$ the volume of the empty space in the container. All of these quantities change with time. In particular, we are given

$$
\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}=-\frac{4}{\pi }\,\text{cm}/\text{s},
$$

which is negative because the distance from the top of the container to the batter surface decreases as we pour the batter into the container.

We want to know $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$ when $r=\frac{3}{2}\,\text{cm}.$

We need to find a relation between $v$ and the variable for which we know the rate of change, which is $h.$ This is given by the formula for the volume of a cone:

$$
v=\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}h.
$$

Before we differentiate the equation with respect to time, note that $r$ also appears in the formula. So, we need to simplify the formula by writing $r$ in terms of $h.$

Note that the cones formed by the container and the batter must be similar. Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{r}{h} & =\frac{R}{H} \\ \frac{r}{h} & =\frac{4}{8} \\ r & =\frac{h}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the volume formula as

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{1}{3}\pi {(\frac{h}{2})}^{2}h \\ v & =\frac{1}{12}\pi {h}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now that we have an equation relating $v$ and $h,$ we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}v & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{12}\pi {h}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{1}{4}\pi {h}^{2}\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want to know $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$ when $r=\frac{3}{2}\,\text{cm}.$ We can compute the value of $h$ at this moment as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2} & =\frac{h}{2} \\ h & =3\,\text{cm}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting the known values, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{1}{4}\pi (3)^{2}(-\frac{4}{\pi }) \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} & =-9\,{\text{cm}}^{3}/\text{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the volume of batter is increasing at a rate of $9\,{\text{cm}}^{3}/\text{s}.$
